item.title: How to Spot OCD, OCPD, and Limerence in Movies
item.description:
OCD

How to Spot OCD, OCPD, and Limerence in Movies

"Whiplash," "As Good As It Gets," and "Vertigo" show how obsession hijacks a mind.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • OCPD is one of the most prevalent personality disorders, driven by rigid perfectionism and need for control.
  • OCD pairs intrusive, unwanted thoughts with ritualistic compulsions meant to relieve anxiety.
  • Limerence is an involuntary romantic obsession that can persist for years without being reciprocated.
  • All three conditions can quietly erode relationships, work, and daily functioning if left untreated.

Movies love exploring obsession. An obsessed protagonist can be one of the most engaging kinds of characters because they will not relent no matter what. Whether it is control, revenge, or love, the character usually has to enter a morally ambiguous situation driven by their obsession, which constantly escalates everything—and often makes for a thrilling couple of hours.

In real life, obsessions can be debilitating, anxiety-causing, and stressful. Obsessions and compulsions come in many different forms that cause suffering for many who have them and contribute to overall distress. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and the phenomenon known as limerence are three types of obsessions that cause relationship conflict, problems at school and work, emotional dysregulation, and can quietly unravel a person’s life if left untreated.

Whiplash
Source: Sony Pictures Entertainment

Distinguishing Between OCPD, OCD, and Limerence in Film

OCPD emerges in late adolescence and is one of the most prevalent personality disorders to this day. OCPD is a persistent pattern of perfectionism and need for order. Sometimes there is almost a morality about it, and an extreme workaholic or a serious Type A personality, for example, can be more susceptible to this disorder.

In "Whiplash" (2014), Terence Fletcher (J.K. Simmons) is the ultimate perfectionist to the point of cruelty. Fletcher is a music teacher obsessed with pushing his students to their breaking point. His obsessive focus on perfection becomes a dangerous and destructive force in the film. For instance, Fletcher slaps his student (Miles Teller) across the face, humiliates him, and throws a chair at him to force him to play a song repeatedly until he gets it exactly to Fletcher’s perfect standards.

As Good As It Gets
Source: Sony Pictures Entertainment

OCD is marked by obsessions that are uncontrolled, intrusive thoughts, followed by repetitive ritualistic behavior and compulsions. For instance, an individual may compulsively wash their hands or have to avoid stepping on a crack, while OCPD involves a need for procedure, detail, and for everything to line up perfectly.

In "As Good As It Gets" (1997), Melvin Udall (Jack Nicholson) is an obsessive-compulsive writer of romantic fiction who’s rude to everyone he meets. His intrusive, unwanted thoughts (harm-avoidance/magical thinking) and rituals (i.e., he can’t step on cracks in the sidewalk) are done to relieve his anxiety, but they drive everyone around him away.

Limerence is an involuntary, intrusive, all-consuming romantic obsession that involves wanting another person to love you that does not and can last for years. In fact, the individual who is the object of the other person’s limerence is usually unaware of the other person’s feelings. Unlike a crush, limerence is almost like a behavioral addiction or maladaptive daydreaming, and its core features are moodiness, loss of control, withdrawal symptoms, and distress.

Vertigo
Source: Paramount Pictures

"Vertigo" (1958) is a good example of limerence. In this Alfred Hitchcock classic, a former police detective (James Stewart) becomes romantically fixated on a woman (Kim Novak) he is hired to follow. He attempts to physically remake her into the idealized image of the woman he lost, to the point of having her dye her hair and wear the same clothes as the other woman. This film is a great portrayal of romantic obsession, manipulation, and the blurring of reality and fantasy.

item.title: Loud Desperation
item.description:
Anxiety

Loud Desperation

The existential search for significance in contemporary society.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • The fear of insignificance causes people to try to remain relevant by continuously posting on social media.
  • The "fake it until you make it" culture is rife with inauthenticity.
  • The internet has exacerbated the performative nature of our lives.

Comedian Marc Maron recently chastised fellow comedian Bill Maher with what he deemed "desperate chasing of relevance," and this notion captured for me something that I've observed in sessions with patients.

In The Fear of Insignificance: Searching for Meaning in the Twenty-First Century, psychoanalyst Carlo Strenger discusses the dread of being invisible — or, egads, merely "ordinary" rather than extraordinary humans — against a cultural backdrop that worships fame, wealth, optimizing, and "maxxing." Because the ideals promoted by our infotainment-based society are inherently unreachable, most of us are "doomed to fail or fall short," a condition that places us on hamster wheels of continual desperation to remain relevant while retaining the facade of looking calm, cool, and collected.

Strenger notes that pop-spirituality and self-help, including the dynamic that Ron Purser decries in his brilliant book McMindfulness: How Mindfulness Became the New Capitalist Spirituality, have replaced religion as our primary coping mechanism and that this replacement ultimately exacerbates our anxiety rather than ameliorating it. Neither our society’s spiritual ideals, nor material ideals, nor reputational ideals are ever attainable, which keeps all of us on hamster wheels chasing relevance, including the celebrities, artists, billionaires and gurus we most admire. Strenger believes that human beings carry a deep need "to matter, make a difference, and feel a significant purpose" within whatever frame of reference is defined as important by their society. Since the birth of the Internet, “living out loud” and deeming oneself a “public figure”, trying always to remain relevant by producing new content (like this blog), appears to be the context, backdrop, or the stage in which and on which we fret.

One hundred seventy-five years ago at Walden Pond, Thoreau observed that most people "lead lives of quiet desperation," a condition absorbed in silence, mowing the lawn and paying a mortgage, while a private hopelessness accumulates week after week. From growing up with a television that had four stations (plus a public access channel) to now existing in a world with billions of sites and apps that transmit simulacra, the quiet desperation that is normal to the human condition according to Thoreau has now magnified into a loud desperation of people trying to remain relevant.

For almost twenty years I have taught classes on authenticity, and I have come to believe that almost everything we do in public, including the way we speak and the clothing that we wear, is performative. This observation updates what psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan called “The split subject.” Lacan proposed that we become alienated from ourselves — split — the moment we are "thrown into language," to borrow Heidegger's phrase: the moment we begin using words to express ourselves rather than cries and smiles. The split I would locate today runs between the self we consider to be authentic, the person we are when we are alone in our bathrooms, and the performative self we present to the world, such as the person we are on social media. My books and workshops give students tools to be more authentic, more congruent, and less hypocritical.

article continues after advertisement

Having dared to update Lacan, now I will update Thoreau as well: Where Thoreau located quiet desperation, I am witnessing a rise à la Marc Maron in what I would call "loud desperation," a general condition affecting a generation that treats every post like another ticket in a perpetual lottery of social relevance and going viral. For me in Los Angeles, this condition becomes especially vivid in the adult children of parents who built something financially substantial — a business, a real estate portfolio, art, music, etc. — something that now includes a family trust that is the result of several generations of labor. For the people in my community who were born sliding into home plate, who grew up surrounded by the spoils of family accomplishment, what I've observed in sessions, from a largely unconscious awareness that they cannot do better than their parents financially, is a desperation to be relevant. However, in contrast to Thoreau's quiet desperation, what I have witnessed today is loud desperation — the loudness is often inadvertent, but it is loud nonetheless.

I do not believe Steve Jobs ever introduced himself by saying, "I'm Steve Jobs, I am a founder," and yet my community remains full of people introducing themselves precisely this way, borrowing the vocabulary of accomplishment before having done the accomplishing. This "fake it until you make it" level of inauthenticity is loudly desperate. OK, so your parents or grandparents worked hard, invested in real estate, and set up funds that enable you to avoid a 9-5 job, but anointing yourself a “Founder” (it costs $750 to start an LLC) or a “Public Figure” is an exaggeration at best. I like what Warren Buffett said, “I’m giving my children enough money to do something but not enough to do nothing.”

Douglas Coupland gave Generation X a determining ditty when he declared that we’re the first generation to have less financial potential than our parents — something documented thirty years later by economist Thomas Piketty in Capital in the Twenty-First Century. Conversely, and somewhat ironically, what we lack in earning potential, thanks to the internet, we’re making up for in social relevance.

But before turning up the volume on your pitch deck or glossy new podcast, just know that all of the money in the world does not and will not insulate anyone from feeling desperately irrelevant. Just ask Perez Hilton or Paris Hilton or any of the influencers desperately going to extremes to capture ten seconds of your attention that they can ultimately transmute into revenue.

article continues after advertisement

For the rest of us... let's just try to keep it quiet.
